formNote: Usually analysed as phono-semantic: 辶 carries the sense of movement and 首 (OC *l̥uʔ) the sound. Reading the “head” as meaningful — orienting, leading — is popular but interpretive.
summary: First a road, and the act of leading someone along it; in classical thought, the self-unfolding course of all things and the path of cultivation. As a verb 道 also means “to say” — the double sense the Daodejing’s first line turns on.
placement: Above both wings, overlooking the whole course of the trajectory.

satellites.title: A Head at the Crossroads
satellites.evidence: Early bronze forms set 首 (head) inside 行, a crossroads, sometimes with a foot or a hand added. The modern 辶 is a later reduction of that movement element.
satellites.caveat: Most specialists take 首 as phonetic. The image of a head moving through a crossroads is evocative, but it is a reading, not a finding.

satellites.title: Path — and Early “Awakening”
satellites.evidence: Buddhist translators used 道 for mārga, “path”, as in 八正道, the Noble Eightfold Path. Early translators also used it for bodhi, “awakening” — hence 得道, “to attain the Way”. Daoist 道 is a self-so cosmic course; Buddhist mārga is a practice that leads out of suffering: one character, two frames.
satellites.caveat: For bodhi, 道 was later largely replaced by the transliteration 菩提 and by 覺.

satellites.title: Road and Current
satellites.evidence: Malay jalan (“road”; jalan hidup, “way of life”) covers the path sense of 道, while aliran (“current, flow”, also “school of thought”) echoes the water imagery the Daodejing uses for the Way: 上善若水, “the highest good is like water”.
satellites.caveat: An analogy. Neither word is a standard Malay rendering of 道 as a philosophical term.

satellites.title: Way and Word
satellites.evidence: 道 is both “way” and “to say”: “the way that can be spoken is not the constant Way”. Greek λόγος likewise joins “word” with “rational order”; French renders 道 simply as la Voie, “the Way”.
satellites.caveat: This analogy uses the familiar “spoken” reading of 道可道. The verbal 道 has also been read as following or guiding a way; the opening is not an uncontested definition of 道 as speech. Greek λόγος and Daoist 道 are not equivalent doctrines.
